pages.text:
*The Bearer's Almanac, Entry 1: Water is never lost. It is only somewhere else.*

On the morning the river did not come, Wen Lan went down to Hollow Pool with two buckets and the firm conviction that the river had simply overslept.

It was a reasonable theory. The Clear River had run past the village of Qingshi every day of the three hundred years the village had kept records, and in all that time it had been late exactly once, during the great mist of her grandmother's girlhood, and had made up for it by arriving with a brass band of frogs. So Wen walked down the terrace stairs in the pearl-grey light with her buckets knocking against her knees, past the rice fields stepped down the hillside like the pages of an enormous green book, and she fully expected to hear the river long before she saw it, the way you hear a neighbor who is clearing his throat.

She heard nothing. The gorge above the village was full of mist, the long pale kind that lies in the Clear River valley until the sun gets high enough to argue with it, and out of the mist rose the dark shoulders of the cliffs and the single thread of the old footbridge. Below the bridge lay Hollow Pool, the great round basin where the river rested before it tumbled on toward the sea. It had been deep enough, when she was small, for the village boys to dive from the high rock and not touch bottom.

It was a bowl of cracked mud now, the color of a dry biscuit, with a dark thumbprint of water in the middle. Around the thumbprint a few dozen silver fish lay in the muck and opened and closed their mouths, patiently, like clerks who have been told that the office is closed and cannot quite believe it.

Wen stood at the edge of the pool with her buckets and said, to nobody, "That is not right."
pages.image: WIDE: Dawn in a Chinese-inspired terraced river valley: Wen, a sixteen-year-old girl with light warm-tan skin, a high black ponytail tied with a faded blue cloth, a pale linen tunic with a grey sash, a dark charcoal wrap skirt over dark trousers and cloth-wrapped boots, stands small at the cracked-mud edge of a dried round pool holding two buckets, stranded silver fish in the mud, rice terraces stepping down the hillside, mist-filled gorge with tall dark cliffs and an old footbridge above.

pages.text:
By the time the sun had burned the mist off the cliffs, half of Qingshi had come down to look. They stood along the dry bank in their straw hats and padded jackets and looked at the pool the way people look at a relative who has said something strange at a wedding.

"Third day," said old Uncle Fang, who kept the village waterwheel and had been counting out loud for three days. "The channels are empty. The wheel hasn't turned since Tuesday. The seedlings on the lower terraces are going yellow, and Granny Ma's goat has started drinking from the soup pot."

"It is only the dry month," said a woman with a baby on her hip, in the voice of someone who needs it to be true. "It happens. The river sleeps. My own grandmother used to say it. Once a lifetime the river sleeps and wakes."

"Your grandmother," said Uncle Fang, "also said the moon was a lamp somebody forgot to put out." He rubbed his chin. "I have kept that wheel for forty years. A river that sleeps still hums. This one has gone silent from the top of the valley to the bottom, like somebody has put a lid on it."

Nobody laughed. Wen, who had been the one to say it was not right, found herself at the back of the crowd with her buckets still in her hands and her face growing warm, because everyone was suddenly looking at the water and not at her, and what she wanted more than anything in the world at that moment was to be useful.

She had always wanted that. It was her one real flaw, as far as she could tell. Other girls her age wanted to be admired or left alone. Wen wanted, with an almost embarrassing ferocity, to be of use.
pages.image: A crowd of Chinese-inspired villagers in straw hats and padded jackets stands along the dry mud bank of an empty round pool looking down at it, an old man with a grey beard pointing at a still wooden waterwheel in the background, Wen with two buckets at the back of the crowd, terraced rice fields yellowing behind, soft morning light.

pages.text:
The crowd drifted off in ones and twos toward the village, muttering about wells. Wen stayed.

She told herself it was to see whether the fish could be moved, and she knelt in the mud at the edge of the last puddle with her skirt hitched up and began scooping the nearest ones into a bucket with her bare hands. They were slippery and cold and astonishingly strong for fish with no water to be strong in, and every time she lifted one it twisted in her palm as if to say, quite clearly, that this was not what it had meant.

"I know," Wen told it. "I know. I am so sorry. I would put you back if there were anywhere to put you."

She put her hand flat on the surface of the puddle, which was no wider than a washing basin and no deeper than her wrist, and for no reason she could have given she shut her eyes and said, in a voice so quiet it was scarcely a voice, "Please."

The water moved.

It did not splash or ripple. It simply rose, in one piece, like a held breath, out of the hollow in the mud and hung in the air in front of her face as a single trembling sphere the size of a melon, bright with the morning, with a small startled fish turning slowly inside it.

Wen did not breathe. The sphere did not breathe either. She could feel it the way she could feel her own hand, a round, cold, attentive weight just beyond her fingertips, and under the weight, very faintly, a long thread of something that went away from her down the valley and up the valley and past the edge of everything she knew, like the string of a kite.

Then her mouth fell open, and the sphere fell with it, in a great undignified splash that soaked her to the knees and sent the fish skidding across the mud in every direction.
pages.image: WIDE: Wen kneels at the edge of a tiny muddy puddle at the bottom of a huge dried pool, her hand raised, a single glowing sphere of water the size of a melon with one small silver fish inside floating in the air in front of her face, huge misty gorge cliffs and a stone footbridge towering above her, her figure small in the vast scene.

pages.text:
She tried it again. She could not help it. She knelt in the wet mud with her heart going like a drum and her hair coming out of its blue cloth, and she held out one hand toward what was left of the puddle and thought, as hard as she had ever thought anything, up.

The puddle rose. Not a sphere this time: a whole shining spiral of water, climbing from the hollow in a turning column as high as her shoulder, then higher, and the mist from the cliffs came down to meet it in soft pale threads and wound itself around the column like silk around a spindle. Droplets lifted off the mud and the cracked rock and hung glittering around her, hundreds of them, each one holding a tiny upside-down morning. She was standing in the middle of a whirlwind of water, and it was not even wet.

For about three seconds she was perfectly, wildly happy. She laughed out loud. The sound went up into the gorge and came back, and the water spun faster to meet it.

Then the cold arrived.

It began at her fingertips, a small hard ache like holding a stone from the bottom of a winter stream, and it climbed her wrists and her forearms with a speed she did not like at all. And somewhere far away, down the valley, she heard a thin dry sound she knew very well: the sound of the village channel, which had been holding one last cupful of the old river, running empty.

She had taken it. She had not meant to, and she had not known she could, but she understood with a sick certainty exactly where the water in her spiral had come from. It was not hers. It had been somebody's. Somebody else's pond, somebody else's cup.

"Oh," said Wen, very small, and the spiral shivered and began to come apart.
pages.image: Wen standing in a whirling spiral of water and soft mist rising from a dried pool bed, hundreds of glittering droplets hanging in the air around her, her ponytail and pale tunic lifted by the movement, her expression a mix of joy and sudden fear, dark cliffs and misty gorge behind, golden morning light.

pages.text:
"Put it back," said a voice from the bank. "Slowly. Do not drop it. Water that is dropped takes a long time to forgive."

Wen turned. At the far end of the pool, where the path came down from the ferry landing, stood a short, wide woman in a faded blue jacket and a conical bamboo hat, leaning on a long ferry pole as though it were the only thing in the world she trusted. She was barefoot. Her face was a map of weather, and she did not look surprised, which Wen found more frightening than if she had.

Wen lowered her hands. The spiral came down by inches, trembling, and folded back into the hollow of the mud, and the fish she had scattered wriggled hopefully toward it. When the last drop had settled she was shaking so hard she had to sit down on the bank.

"Auntie Mo," she said. Her teeth were chattering. "I did not know. I swear I did not know I could do that."

"No," said Auntie Mo, who had ferried the whole valley across the Clear River for thirty years and had never been known to say anything she did not mean. "I did not think you did." She came across the cracked mud with her pole clicking and crouched by Wen, and took Wen's hands in her own two hard brown ones and turned them over. On the tips of three of Wen's fingers lay a faint white bloom, like the first frost on a window.

Mo looked at it for a long time. "So it is true," she said, almost to herself.

"What is true?"

"That the river has been stopped upstream by hands, not weather." Mo let go. "And that your mother would have known exactly what to do about it."
pages.image: Auntie Mo, a short wide sturdy woman with medium-brown weathered skin, grey hair in a bun under a conical bamboo hat, a faded blue cotton jacket, bare feet and a long bamboo ferry pole, crouches on a cracked mud bank holding Wen's hands to inspect them, Wen sitting with a blue cloth in her black ponytail and a pale linen tunic, a dry round pool and misty cliffs behind them.
